h1: Whisky glassware: tulip glass, tumbler or highball glass
title: Whisky Glassware Guide | Craft Beer School
desc: Which whisky glass to use and why: tulip nosing glasses, tumblers and highball glasses, how shape changes aroma and what to choose for home.
teaser: The glass changes what you smell. Pick it for how you are drinking the whisky tonight.
standfirst: Whisky can be drunk from almost any glass, but the shape changes how much aroma reaches your nose and how the drink feels. Three glasses cover nearly every way of drinking whisky.
sections:
Most of what we call flavour is actually smell. A glass that gathers aroma and directs it towards your nose shows more of a whisky than one that lets it drift away. The shape of the bowl and the width of the rim make a real difference.

The same principle works for beer and wine. Our guide to beer glassware explains why bowl shape matters for hop aroma. Our guide to wine tasting for beginners applies it to wine.

A tulip shaped glass has a rounded bowl that narrows towards the rim. The bowl lets you swirl the whisky. The narrow rim concentrates aroma at your nose. The Glencairn glass and the copita, a stemmed glass borrowed from sherry, are well-known examples.

This is the glass for tasting neat whisky or whisky with a few drops of water. Distillers and blenders use similar glasses every day. If you buy one type of glass for serious tasting, make it this one.

Hold a tulip glass by the base or stem rather than the bowl. Warm hands heat the whisky, which pushes more alcohol vapour at your nose. Swirl gently, nose with your mouth slightly open and take short sniffs rather than one long one. These small habits make a bigger difference than the brand of glass.

The tumbler, also called a rocks glass or old fashioned glass, is short and wide with a heavy base. It is the classic whisky glass in films and bars. Its wide rim lets aroma escape quickly, which makes it less good for close nosing.

It is excellent for whisky on the rocks, whisky with a splash of water and short cocktails like the old fashioned. A big ice cube fits well. The heavy base feels good in the hand. For relaxed drinking, it is the most comfortable glass.

A highball glass is tall and narrow, holding around 300 to 350 ml. It is made for whisky with soda or another mixer over plenty of ice. The tall shape keeps bubbles lively and leaves room for ice.

In hot Indian weather the highball glass is often the most useful whisky glass you can own. Our guide to whisky tasting for beginners explains why a long, cold drink shows lighter whiskies well.

Very thick, heavy cut glass tumblers look impressive but can be clumsy for tasting. Very wide brandy balloons let high strength alcohol hit the nose too hard and blur the aroma. Plastic and paper cups carry their own smells.

Chilled glasses straight from the freezer dull aroma when drinking neat. Save cold glasses for highballs.

Your glass choice also depends on whether you add ice or water. A few drops of water in a tulip glass open up aroma in a strong whisky, because dilution releases some aroma compounds that the alcohol holds back. Use a dropper or a teaspoon so you control the amount.

Ice works differently. It chills the whisky, softens the alcohol and mutes aroma at the same time. That is why ice belongs in a tumbler or highball glass and not in a nosing glass. In Indian summers many people prefer whisky with ice, which is perfectly fine. Simply pick the glass that suits the drink you are making.

Wash whisky glasses in hot water with very little detergent and rinse well. Detergent residue and dishwasher rinse aids leave a film that kills aroma and can taste soapy. Air dry upside down on a rack or polish with a clean, lint-free cloth.

Store glasses upright in a closed cupboard. Stored upside down on a shelf they can pick up smells from the wood or paint. Before a tasting, smell each empty glass. Any smell other than nothing means rinse again.

Start with two or four tulip nosing glasses for tasting, a set of tumblers for relaxed drinking and a few highball glasses for summer. That covers almost every way you will drink whisky.

If you only buy one, choose by how you usually drink. Mostly neat? A tulip glass. Mostly with ice and soda? A highball glass. You can always add more later.
faqs: What is the best glass for tasting whisky?
A tulip shaped nosing glass, such as a Glencairn or copita, gathers aroma best for neat whisky or whisky with a little water.
Is a tumbler good for whisky?
It is ideal for whisky on the rocks or short cocktails. Its wide rim lets aroma escape, so it is less suited to careful tasting.
Not for neat whisky, as cold dulls aroma. A chilled highball glass is fine for whisky with soda and ice.
